note: Argues outcome auditing is legally permitted and necessary because bias often sits outside the code, which supports the case for external review.
title: Auditing Algorithms for Discrimination
journal: University of Pennsylvania Law Review Online

reading.body:
Fairness cannot be guaranteed by code alone, because bias often enters through social conditions outside the software, so outcomes must be audited after deployment.

Kim's argument is that technical fairness methods, such as randomization or fixed decision rules, cannot ensure unbiased results. Carefully built systems can still reproduce existing prejudice or structural disadvantage. The practical response is to inspect how systems actually behave, because only observed effects reveal discrimination. Kim also concludes that this kind of auditing is legally permitted, and reads Ricci v. DeStefano narrowly, as covering adverse action against identifiable people by race rather than prospective changes to remove bias.

For AI specifically, this shifts fairness from a design property to an operational one. A model that passes review at build time can still produce discriminatory outcomes once it meets real data and real decisions. That makes ongoing outcome monitoring and correction a recurring cost, not a one-time engineering task, and it puts the burden on whoever operates the system after it ships.

The data covers one 2017 law review essay and its argument, with 62 citations. It does not measure how often audits are performed, what they cost, or whether Kim's legal reading has been tested in court. It also says nothing about compute, buildings, or power, so no claim about infrastructure can be drawn from it.

explain_beginner: Kim's paper argues that fair code is not enough to stop discrimination. Bias can enter through social conditions and structural inequality, not only through programming choices. Methods such as randomization or fixed rules cannot promise unbiased results. Even carefully built systems may carry forward old prejudices. So the paper says we must watch how systems actually behave and study their outcomes. This kind of auditing is necessary to find and correct unfair outcomes. It is also allowed by law, according to Kim. The point matters because unfair outcomes can go unnoticed without outcome review.
explain_business: For executives, this paper means that fairness cannot be guaranteed by good design or technical safeguards alone. Automated decisions may still produce biased results because bias can come from broader social conditions. The practical step is to audit actual outcomes after deployment and use external review where needed. Kim argues this is legally permitted, so companies can act voluntarily to find and correct bias. A key legal point is that algorithms may be revised prospectively to remove discrimination. The decision this informs is to fund ongoing outcome monitoring and correction, rather than treating fairness as a single engineering task.
explain_practitioner: Kim's essay replies to Kroll and colleagues, who favored technical fairness methods over transparency. Kim argues that for discrimination, such methods cannot stand alone. Bias often arises from social processes outside the software, so randomization or preset decision constraints cannot ensure unbiased results. Carefully built systems can still reproduce existing prejudice or structural disadvantage. The practical response is to inspect real outcomes, not just design, because only observed effects reveal discrimination. Kim examines law and concludes that auditing is permitted. The contrary reading, Kim says, misinterprets Ricci v. DeStefano. That ruling was narrow, about adverse action against identifiable people by race, while prospective algorithm changes to remove bias remain lawful.
